notes.title: Capture actionable failure context without disclosing secrets
notes.core: Exception detail messages are developer diagnostics: capture the relevant invalid value, permitted boundary and operation context so investigators can distinguish failure modes, but never copy credentials, secrets or regulated payloads into exceptions or logs.
rules: For a rejected range, retain the index and valid bounds or a stable non-sensitive error code instead of only saying invalid.
Capture relevant causal parameters and invariant state at the point of failure; do not rely on being able to reproduce the input later.
Keep exception detail messages concise and oriented to developers, rather than substituting them for localized client-facing errors.
Never place raw authentication tokens, passwords, full customer documents or cryptographic keys in exception messages or toString.
Offer typed exception construction with safe structured values when repeated failure types need consistent diagnostic context.
Preserve cause chains and trace/correlation IDs only after redaction and cardinality/retention review; avoid logging the same exception repeatedly.
nuance: A dangerous raw input can be better represented by its length or classification rather than its literal value.
Stack traces and metrics may be exported across trust boundaries; exception messages are not inherently private.
Message strings are not a stable machine-readable API; downstream classification should use typed exception fields or explicit codes.
An exception constructor should not unexpectedly throw while formatting its diagnostic data.
A precise bound in a message does not itself ensure that sensitive metadata is approved for telemetry.
notes.misconception: The safest error is just “failed”, or conversely all input values should be logged because debugging requires them.
notes.production_context: A ledger pagination failure records a safe page offset, allowed range and trace ID but never writes a session token or customer identity into the error detail.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 retains Throwable messages and cause chains; modern structured logging still requires explicit redaction and approved retention boundaries.

notes.title: Preserve state invariants on failed operations
notes.core: An operation should ordinarily leave its receiver in its original well-defined state if it fails: validate up front, compute before mutation, publish a fully prepared copy atomically, or explicitly define and test a compensation protocol where atomicity is impossible.
rules: Validate public inputs and ranges before changing mutable state so errors cannot leave partially updated fields.
Move calculations that may throw before the first mutation when those calculations do not depend on the mutated state.
Prepare an immutable snapshot or temporary working copy and publish it only after all intended checks and transformations succeed.
Use transaction semantics when the unit of work spans a transactional store, and document which side effects a rollback cannot undo.
Where failure atomicity cannot be afforded, document the post-failure validity guarantee and provide a well-specified recovery or reconciliation step.
Test both success and every failure point, including overflow, callbacks and concurrent state transitions.
nuance: A Java in-memory snapshot can prevent partial object mutation but does not roll back email, network or payment effects.
A volatile snapshot reference establishes publication visibility but does not automatically make multi-step external commits atomic.
Copy-then-publish has allocation and contention costs; choose based on invariants and profile rather than dogma.
Concurrent actors require a linearization or conflict policy beyond individual method failure atomicity.
Compensating actions in a distributed Saga may fail, so reconciliation and idempotency are separate obligations.
notes.misconception: If a method eventually throws an exception, the JVM automatically rolls back all modifications it performed.
notes.production_context: A merchant-credit configuration is validated and copied into a prepared immutable snapshot before swapping the active version; remote settlement is handled by idempotency and reconciliation, not a fictional in-memory rollback.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 record/value models and AtomicReference updates can support immutable snapshot publication; external side effects still require domain-specific transactional design.

notes.title: Handle exceptions with an observable policy, never silent dismissal
notes.core: Every caught exception requires an intentional response: recover with a proven safe fallback, translate and preserve its cause, propagate it, or document why ignoring a specifically bounded cleanup failure is harmless. Empty generic catch blocks hide errors and destroy evidence.
rules: Never catch an exception just to continue silently; explicit exception policy should be visible in code and tests.
Only use a fallback if the domain guarantees that the fallback preserves correctness and does not falsely claim a completed side effect.
Propagate or translate unexpected failures with the cause intact; do not turn infrastructure timeouts into ordinary empty responses.
Document narrowly justified suppression of secondary cleanup failures and consider reporting at an appropriate diagnostic level.
Preserve the thread interruption signal when catching InterruptedException if termination/cancellation is not being propagated immediately.
Avoid catching Throwable or Error for routine business flow, and ensure recovery loops are bounded.
nuance: Try-with-resources adds cleanup failures as suppressed exceptions and generally retains the primary cause.
A timeout during a nonessential suggestion step may use a documented safe default, unlike a payment-capture timeout.
Blindly logging and rethrowing at every layer can multiply alerts; choose an owning observability boundary.
An ignored cleanup exception may be acceptable only when no correctness or resource-integrity obligation depends on successful cleanup.
Java virtual threads support interruption and cancellation; a swallowed interrupt can obstruct structured task shutdown.
notes.misconception: Since the system keeps running after an empty catch, the exception was harmless.
notes.production_context: A reconciliation job propagates a gateway failure rather than marking the transfer settled; an optional cosmetic enrichment step may use a documented stale snapshot after a bounded timeout.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 try-with-resources, interruption and virtual-thread cancellation make explicit recovery and cleanup semantics important; no runtime automatically validates a silent fallback.

notes.title: Synchronize shared mutable state for both visibility and atomic transitions
notes.core: Shared mutable state needs a defined visibility and concurrency contract. Use synchronized operations or suitable atomic/concurrent classes for compound transitions, and volatile for visibility of independent reads/writes where compound read-modify-write is not required.
rules: Establish happens-before relationships with a shared lock, volatile access or concurrency utilities; atomic primitive reads alone do not establish timely visibility.
Use volatile for a stop flag or immutable snapshot publication, but do not treat volatile++ as an atomic counter increment.
Use AtomicInteger/AtomicLong or a lock for compound counters; synchronize related invariants under the same policy.
Prefer immutable message passing and concurrent collections over unrelated mutable fields shared between workers.
Do not use Thread.stop to cancel tasks; use interruption or explicit cooperative stop with documented propagation.
Test state transitions, contention and shutdown, while recognizing deterministic tests alone cannot prove absence of all races.
nuance: An AtomicReference holding an immutable snapshot protects publication, not automatically coordination of two external side effects.
ConcurrentHashMap atomic compute operations and simple get-then-put sequences have different guarantees.
A lock protects invariants only when all accesses that participate in those invariants follow the same locking discipline.
Java 21 virtual threads change thread management costs but not the Java memory model.
LongAdder is useful for contended metrics, not a drop-in linearizable precise counter snapshot in all algorithms.
notes.misconception: Because boolean reads or int assignments are atomic, no synchronization is needed for communication or compound updates.
notes.production_context: A distributed payment adapter stores a volatile immutable configuration snapshot and updates account-level in-memory counters with AtomicLong, while using durable idempotency for cross-service correctness.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 virtual threads and modern atomic/concurrent primitives retain ordinary JMM visibility and synchronization rules; do not confuse low-cost threads with automatic thread safety.

notes.title: Keep unknown callbacks outside synchronization boundaries
notes.core: Protect the smallest necessary shared state transition with a lock and invoke external or overridable code only after leaving the synchronized region. Snapshot listeners under the lock, then notify outside it; avoid assuming unknown callbacks are fast, safe or nonblocking.
rules: Never call an untrusted listener, overridable hook or client-supplied function while holding an internal monitor when possible.
Take an immutable observer snapshot inside a synchronized block and dispatch notifications only after releasing the lock.
Choose CopyOnWriteArrayList when listener churn is low relative to notification reads, evaluating allocation costs.
Document whether callbacks can subscribe/unsubscribe during a notification and which event snapshot they observe.
Keep synchronized critical sections short to reduce lock contention, deadlock opportunities and unexpected blocking.
If callbacks must be asynchronous, specify ordering, delivery failure and backpressure; moving work to a thread pool alone is not an outbox.
nuance: A synchronized callback may reenter the same monitor and mutate a live iteration, producing surprising behavior despite reentrant monitors.
A snapshot-based callback delivery policy does not guarantee exactly-once delivery or transactionality with database state.
CopyOnWriteArrayList iterators are snapshot-based but copying on every mutation can be expensive for high-churn registrations.
External callbacks may block indefinitely or call into another lock, inducing deadlocks; design timeouts and policy only where safe.
Virtual-thread pinning/monitor behavior depends on the JDK version; do not claim all synchronized use is harmless or universally expensive.
notes.misconception: An internal synchronized block makes any arbitrary observer callback safe, because only one thread can be inside it.
notes.production_context: A settlement event dispatcher snapshots registered subscribers under its private monitor and invokes handlers afterward; durable delivery uses a separate outbox and retries.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 provides CopyOnWriteArrayList and virtual threads; callback escape from monitors and explicit delivery semantics remain essential independent of scheduling model.
